statement: In US Medicaid enrollees aged 18 to 64 who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months of continuous treatment and stayed enrolled for the next 6 months, about 5 in 100 had at least one medically treated drug overdose, and between 4 and 5 in 10 visited an emergency department, in the 6 months after stopping, in one claims-based cohort study with no group that stayed on treatment (Williams et al., 2020, read from the online-first version). In the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims of 2013–2017, 8,996 people met these conditions (61.0% women, 91.5% White, 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day). Stopping meant a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out, and the 6 months were counted from the last day of supply. In those 6 months, 464 people (5.2%; 95% CI 4.7 to 5.6, editors' calculation) had at least one medically treated overdose, opioid or non-opioid (5.1% to 5.5% in the four groups by length of treatment; 5.6% among the 8,077 with a recorded diagnosis of opioid use disorder); 41.2% to 48.6% had at least one emergency department visit, 11.3% to 13.9% at least one hospital admission, and 19.1% to 25.9% filled a prescription for a full-agonist opioid, which the authors read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care. Against people treated for 6 to 9 months (4,126), those treated for 15 to 18 months (931) had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.86), hospital admission (0.79, 0.64 to 0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.67, 0.56 to 0.80), and those treated for 12 to 15 months lower odds of emergency visits (0.84) and opioid prescriptions (0.84), but the odds of overdose did not differ (15 to 18 months 1.04, 0.75 to 1.44, an interval that allows odds about 25% lower to 44% higher, editors' reading). Overdose after stopping was more likely with a recorded psychiatric diagnosis (odds ratio 1.61), alcohol use disorder (2.02) or another drug use disorder (1.51), and less likely in women (0.65). Because no group continued buprenorphine, the study cannot say whether stopping raised these risks compared with staying on treatment; the records do not say why anyone stopped; and the comparison of durations is adjusted only for age, sex, race, plan type, recorded diagnoses and starting dose, which the authors say leaves residual confounding possible. Deaths are not recorded: anyone who died, or lost Medicaid for any other reason, in the 6 months after stopping was excluded (3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the study window, 30.5%, editors' calculation), so fatal overdoses are not counted, as the authors say, and the figures are not the full risk after stopping. Only overdoses billed to Medicaid were counted, and the code list is printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, which leaves out T40.0 to T40.4, the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, methadone and other opioids (study card note), although the same sentence says that opioid overdoses were counted; the codes used are in an online table (S1) that was not on file. The people studied had all stayed in treatment at least 6 months, a minority the authors describe as likely relatively stable, so the figures may not apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid. The discussion's statement that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures and sets this study's medically treated overdoses beside death rates from another study, so it is not used here. Death rates during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment, from a review of cohort studies, are a separate answer (see the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What happens after stopping Suboxone? In US Medicaid records of 8,996 people who stopped buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after 6 to 18 months of treatment, about 5 in 100 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor or hospital in the next 6 months. In those 6 months, 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital, and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid. People who had been on buprenorphine for 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than people who stopped after 6 to 9 months, but no fewer overdoses. Nobody in the study stayed on treatment, so it cannot say whether stopping raised the risk, and the records do not say why people stopped. People who died, or lost their Medicaid cover, in those 6 months were left out, so overdoses that killed people are not counted. Deaths during and after treatment are covered in a separate answer.
population: Adults aged 18 to 64 in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database (2013–2017; contributing states not named) who began a new buprenorphine episode for opioid use disorder, stayed on it continuously for 6 to 18 months, then stopped, and stayed enrolled in Medicaid for the 6 months afterwards: 8,996 people (61.0% women; 91.5% White; 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day); people also covered by Medicare were excluded
exposure: Stopping buprenorphine (a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out) after 6–9 (4,126 people), 9–12 (2,440), 12–15 (1,499) or 15–18 months (931) of continuous treatment, by days supplied in pharmacy claims; the 6 months of follow-up counted from the last day of supply
comparator: No group that continued buprenorphine. The longer-treatment groups against the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race (White or not), Medicaid plan type, recorded psychiatric, alcohol and other drug use disorder diagnoses, and starting dose
outcome: At least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid (ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50), at least one emergency department visit, at least one inpatient admission, and at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription, in Medicaid claims in the 6 months after stopping; deaths not recorded
magnitude: Williams et al. (2020). Flow: 26,576 with a new continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop (39.4%, editors) and 3,159 who stopped too late in the study window removed; 12,936 who stopped within the window; 3,940 (30.5%, editors) removed for incomplete enrolment in the 6 months after stopping; 8,996 analysed (6–9 months 4,126; 9–12 months 2,440; 12–15 months 1,499; 15–18 months 931). Six-month outcomes across the four groups, unadjusted: emergency department visit 41.2–48.6% (abstract 42.1–49.9%), inpatient admission 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescription 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdose 5.1–5.5%; overall overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6, editors). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% against 48.6% (p < 0.001), admissions 11.3% against 13.9% (p < 0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% against 25.9% (p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios against 6–9 months (Table 2): 15–18 months, admission 0.79 (0.64–0.99), emergency visit 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescription 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Overdose, other terms in the same model: women 0.65 (0.54–0.79); psychiatric diagnosis 1.61 (1.32–1.96); alcohol use disorder 2.02 (1.47–2.79); non-opioid drug use disorder 1.51 (1.22–1.86); starting dose 1.00 per mg (0.97–1.04). Sensitivity analysis (8,077 with a recorded opioid use disorder diagnosis): 15–18 against 6–9 months, emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); odds of overdose equivalent across groups, 5.6% overall.

evidence.locator: Figure 1 note (p. 2); Methods › Study Design and Participants, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 2–3)
evidence.extracted: MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims, 2013–2017, about 12 million enrollees a year. Adults aged 18–64 starting a new buprenorphine episode (no buprenorphine claim in the previous 60 days; formulations for pain excluded), continuously on it for at least 180 days and continuously enrolled for 6 months after stopping; buprenorphine started before 1 January 2017. Stopping was a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied by the last fill, dated to the last day of medication coverage. Groups by days supplied: 6–9 months (180–270 days), 9–12 (271–364), 12–15 (365–455) and 15–18 (456–545); the 6–9-month group is the reference.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could change the figures materially (card sc_williams_2020, ROBINS-I serious): 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped (30.5%) were excluded for losing Medicaid in the 6 months after stopping, a group that includes everyone who died; overdoses count only if billed to Medicaid; the printed code list leaves out the opioid codes, and the table of the codes used was not read.

inconsistency.note: One study; the four duration groups give similar overdose rates (5.1% to 5.5%).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled; the statement says the figures leave out deaths, may not apply to people who stop early or are outside Medicaid, and come with no group that stayed on treatment.

imprecision.note: 464 overdoses; the overall share has a narrow interval (4.7% to 5.6%). The duration comparison for overdose is imprecise (0.75 to 1.44) and is worded as no detected difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all four outcomes are reported for every comparison, including the null overdose result.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (how many people had each event in the 6 months after stopping): starts low; down one level for risk of bias, because exclusions that include every death and an overdose definition that cannot be checked could change the figures materially: very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. The comparisons by length of treatment are associations in the same records, open to confounding by why and when people stopped, and are not rated separately; the authors concede the design cannot show cause. Nothing here compares stopping with continuing: deaths during and after treatment are the subject of the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine, which rests on a review of cohort studies and measures deaths, not treated overdoses; the two do not conflict. Status: single study.

verification.flag_note: Question 16 of round pdf-2026-11-26. Read from the online-first version (AJP in Advance, 8 pages); the print version (Am J Psychiatry 177(2), 117–124) was not read, and the online supplement (Tables S1 to S3: overdose codes, diagnosis codes, sensitivity analysis) was not on file: Table S1 would settle the code list. Not read: Larochelle et al. (2018), Annals of Internal Medicine 169, 137–145, the source of the authors' comparison with annual rates after a past overdose. Whether stopping raises the risk would need a cohort that links deaths and includes people who stay on buprenorphine. Kept consistent with the answer on deaths during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment (Sordo et al., 2017), which this claim points to and does not repeat.
